comments.text: I'm near 70 years old and have been told by various dentist thru the decades that my teeth are in awful shape and I need urgent procedures done to save them. From a "sales" perspective their are questions to gauge how much the customer is willing/able to spend. When's the last time you visit a dentist? Do you floss after every meal? Filling a patient form that's like a credit app. Does the dentist really need those questions accurately answered? Why can't he just go by a thorough exam of the mouth. The population in the rest of the globe aren't walking around toothless by 40, or  having implants done. The last few years so much advertisement is for whole mouth implants. Geesh!  For a dentist, it must be a lot easier working on healthy mouths that don't need the procedure and reap the benefit of improving your skills while getting  paid for  your training venture.  The dentist educator, Elle Phillips, authored books and video's discusses reasonable low cost approach and makes more common sense than current American dental practice. It's gotten so bad that when I'm told I have more than 2 cavities I go to a different dentist for a check up.  I've notice in social media comments that now more and more dentist aren't discussing with the client what's needed-they're just going a head and doing it the same day. It is not a requirement in many places to be a dentist to own a dental shop. I guess the term that describes this is private equity. If your a corporation you'll always be looking for people with the talent that attains confidence from the public fast, a top producer-compared to peers,. I don't see them getting around a commission pay structure and if the corporations all about money-run the dentists the same way you'd run a sales floor.

comments.text:
Private equity firms are buying up hospitals, & firing staff, leading to a 13% rise in death rates in those ERs. Meanwhile billions in investor gains are paid out.
#hospital 
How it works:

A private equity firm identifies a hospital—often a community hospital in rural or underserved areas.

The firm buys it (loans are placed directly on the hospital's books)

Because of that debt, (on the hospital not the firm) the hospital is forced to make quick cash to cover the interest payments.

Cost cutting measures take place: reduced salaries, staff levels cut & services scaled back

Nurses become overworked, support teams exhausted and care level drops.

For example:

Steward Health Care was purchased in 2010, Steward then expanded aggressively but filed for bankruptcy in 2024 with $9 billion of debt, after closing hospitals in Massachusetts and not paying vendors.
#Massachusetts 
 The CEO reportedly purchased a $40 million yacht during the cost cutting measures, staff cuts and hospital closures.

Private equity has invested over $1 trillion in health care in the past decade, and now owns or operates around 500 hospitals nationwide, which is almost 30% of all for-profit facilities - and control 25% of emergency rooms across the country.
#healthcare 
A study by researchers from Harvard Medical School, the University of Pittsburgh, and the University of Chicago, Analyzed over 1 million ER visits at 49 private equity hospitals from 2009 to 2019, compared to 293 non private equity facilities.

Here's what they found:

🏨ER salary spending dropped 18.2%.

🏨Intensive care unit salary spending dropped 15.9%.

🏨Hospital-wide full-time employees dropped by 11.6%.

🏨ER deaths rose 13%

🏨2.7% rise in deaths post operations

🏨25% rise in hospital complications like infections and falls.

In cases like Prospect Medical Holdings, owned by Leonard Green & Partners, aggressive expansion because of the $1.6 billion in debt they racked up - led to service cuts and closures.

Investors pocketed $645–658 million (including $424 million to Leonard Green shareholders) in dividends and fees during service cuts, layoffs, multiple hospital closures ( in Texas, Pennsylvania), and filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in January 2025.
